This is another review where I wish there was a "mixed" option, because I don't really know how to feel about this title.

On the one hand, even on medium settings, the game looks stunning. The character models are really detailed (especially with mods). Water looks great. The weather effects are lovely too, and the survival mechanics are actually pretty cool. Food poisoning, venom, exposure, thirst; you can die to a lot of different things in this game. It really does feel like a survival experience, which is something most survival games these days lack.

However... I have a couple of major gripes with the game, combat being the biggest one.

The smaller of the two gripes is progression; the game doesn't make any real effort to show you the map and it only just tries to introduce crafting certain facilities to you via... I believe it was called Journies. It feels hands off in a way that basically leaves you floundering for the first few hours. I died several times in the desert because I accidentally dropped my water skin or respawned in the Siptah region that resulted in me getting chased around by wildlife and monsters nearly constantly. It was funny at first but quickly became grating.

I don't know if I'm missing something or not, but progression feels... esoteric? And quite slow. The menus aren't exactly intuitive, especially the "Knowledge" tab. Even after almost 20 hours, I still don't really understand how it works.

The second gripe is, admittedly, made in part due to personal preference. However, the other part is also technical, too. This game has Souls-like combat. Lock-on camera, stamina, dodge rolls, light/heavy attacks, etc. Anyone that reads my reviews or otherwise knows me personally knows I LOATHE Souls games. While it wouldn't be fair to say CE is an exact copy, it borrows enough from Souls to make me dislike it. I don't even like this style of combat when it's done well, let alone how this game does it.

That was the personal preference part. This next part is the technical half; the combat in this game feels, at best, inoffensive. At worse, it feels actively awful. For reference, I played this exclusively in Singleplayer mode. If you thought Dark Souls had phantom range, this game has it and then some; you'll straight up get hit by attacks when enemies aren't even facing you. This is even worse with human enemies using two-handed weapons. I'm talking "my back is to you but I still killed you anyway" shenanigans. And apparently, this game's combat was revamped a number of times in the past. Unbelievable!

Attacks have insanely long recovery frames; you will observe both your character and enemy NPCs just awkwardly standing there after taking a swing for, no joke, like 2 to 3 seconds. The weapons range from feeling okay to just plain weak. Enemies often don't even respond to your attacks in a meaningful way.

There is no real way to tell how powerful an enemy is. You can have two hostile NPCs that look almost exactly the same, all the way down to wearing almost no armor, but one can die in 2-3 hits while the other's health bar barely gets scratched by anything you do to them. You can encounter this issue as early as the first parts of the map when you start playing. There's a reason why games like Palworld show your enemy's level so you know what you're getting into. Otherwise, it feels like artificial difficulty even on Civilized (easy) mode.

Exploration is fun... to a point. The map is huge but there doesn't seem to be any practical way to traverse it. Put simply, it takes forever to travel anywhere and if you die, you spawn back at the default spawn or your bed if you built one. Does the game tell you how to get around so you can explore the map better? What do you think? Pair this with you needing to travel fairly far to find certain materials and this becomes a problem very quickly. I had a hard time even just finding iron because of this, plus the game not telling you where you can locate it in significant amounts. It created a feeling of just being stuck unless I want to use a guide.

While I do like that the game doesn't hold your hand, a sandbox should at least introduce tools to you in an intuitive way to help make figuring out what to do with the sand in question a little bit more sensible. Even EvE Online does a better job of this and that game is known for the "Learning curve? How about Learning Cliff" meme.

I can't say I flat-out don't recommend this game because it does a number of things right, but for me? I can't get over how difficult it is to figure out how to progress or where to go for materials, and the awful combat system where every enemy is seemingly able to hit you at ranges that should, by all accounts, be deemed as impossible.

I shudder to think about what the multiplayer experience is like.

Conan Exiles Enhanced is much more than just a survival game. With the move to Unreal Engine 5, the game received a major visual upgrade, but what makes it really interesting is the freedom and depth it offers.

The game has a lot of farming, crafting and progression. You gather resources, build and upgrade your base, craft equipment, capture and manage thralls, explore dangerous areas, fight bosses and discover the lore of the world. There is a lot to learn and plenty of things to work towards, so it can be quite complex, especially when you start going deeper into the game.

One of the best additions in Enhanced is the merged worlds. The Exiled Lands and Isle of Siptah can exist on the same server**, and you can travel between them with the same character. You can build, explore and progress across both maps without having to start over with another character.

The building system is another huge part of the game. If you're someone who loves building, you can spend hundreds of hours creating huge castles, villages, cities or completely crazy constructions. Enhanced also makes crafting and building more convenient by allowing you to use resources from nearby storage and follower inventories.

And then there are mods. This is where Conan Exiles can become almost a completely different game. Whether you're a building addict looking for more construction pieces, someone who loves character customization, or someone looking for new gameplay systems, there are mods for almost every playstyle. Enhanced officially supports mods and has an updated Mod Dev Kit.

The roleplay potential is also enormous. You can create your own character, build your own story and interact with other players. Depending on the server, you can find serious RP, casual RP, fantasy communities and even adult/erotic roleplay for players who are interested in that type of experience.

The story and lore are also worth discovering. You can simply play your own survival adventure, but if you take the time to explore the world, discover its characters, ruins, religions and secrets, there is a lot more going on beneath the surface.

The game isn't perfect. There are bugs, some mechanics can be complicated, and the amount of farming and progression can sometimes feel overwhelming. But that's also part of what makes Conan Exiles so addictive.

Build, explore, farm, fight, capture thralls, customize your character, install mods, roleplay or simply create your own adventure.

There are very few survival games that give you this much freedom.

If you like survival games with a lot of content, complexity and customization, Conan Exiles Enhanced is definitely worth trying.

I give Conan Exiles Enhanced, with no mods, a 5 out of 10. If you add mods to bring it up to the standards of games released in the last 10 years, it is a 7 out of 10.

First off, add a minimap because it does not come standard, and the screen-wide map is a huge pain. I also opted for an extra toolbar because you will be using weapons, tools, and items constantly, and 8 slots is not enough. Finally, I added a hearthstone to get back to my base. This one isn't necessary, and I didn't count it toward the score. I did this because I am old, married, a father, and working on an advanced degree, and I don't have time to travel to the ends of a massive map with no way to get home. Hearthstone saves time.

Not having a minimap to find friends or a compass to show directions is a huge pain. (Side note: there is a compass in the game; I found it 30 hours later. It is off by default in the settings. Yay.) This review is from the perspective of a survival-builder enjoyer. I play with a friend on a dedicated server and played PVE. I cannot say anything in good faith about PVP.

I would recommend this game if you want something to sink a lot of time into and don't mind looking things up. However, if you want to beat it without the PRIMA Cheat Guide, stay away. I ended up recommending it because I think it is fun and worth the sale price. Get it on sale; it's a $20 game through and through, not a nickel more. Spend 20 hours in it, and you've gotten your money's worth. Beyond that, though, the frustration sets in.

Starting with the positive.

When the game hits, it is awesome. Stunning vistas unfold as the sun rises after a dark night. The lighting gives the world atmosphere and can make a place terrifying or inviting. Riding a horse through the desert with dust kicking up behind you makes you feel like Indiana Jones on some awesome adventure. The dungeons, caves, and camps feel unique, and there are so many adventures to be had getting “friends” to work at your base.

The game is beautiful, and there was clearly some time and love spent crafting these locations. Basebuilding is okay. The default sandstone is very meh, but you can make a town of people, which is pretty neat. My friend and I just made a large building because we are unimaginative.

If you want an adventure that doesn't hold your hand, and you want to build and just ♥♥♥♥ around, this game is recommended.

Now to the negative.

There is very little guidance. Journeys guide you through aspects of the game like building, religion, and crafting, but they don't guide you toward the main goal: getting the bracelet off. You are set free on 500 acres of desert, jungle, and Norway and told to get the bracelet off. Good luck figuring that out without Googling it.

The game gives vague ideas about what to accomplish. In fact, the main guy who tells you how to get the bracelet off tells you wrong. He even mentions an artifact that isn't in the game; it is unfinished content.

This extends to crafting. There is some help getting materials, but good luck figuring out where they are. There is little help finding brimstone, star metal, black ice, and all the other things they fill your inventory with. Yes, black ice is in the mountains. But that is like half the map. Finding it becomes random trial and error.

There is so much useless stuff in this game to weigh you down that it is insane. Get the treasure room up ASAP for chests because you will need a lot of them. Not too many, though; the game has a limit on how many containers it can search in a base, and crafting benches count too.

The crafting also feels sad because you outpace it so quickly. Why not give us a way to upgrade the compass to see allies? A minimap item? What about a straw for your waterskin so you don't have to drink it every five seconds?

Don't plan on doing a lot of looting either; you have a tiny encumbrance window. Armor, weapons, and a few health pots, and you cannot carry anything else. Why? This is unfun. Some armor gives more carry capacity, but you quickly outpace it, and you don't want to wear light armor into battle. A backpack, dungeon item, or anything that meaningfully increased capacity would have fixed this.

Combat can feel clunky. You will be stunlocked and killed if fighting more than one person, and it isn't fun. Not all weapons are created equal, either. Find what you enjoy and stick with it. Except thrown weapons; they suck. If you throw them, they're gone forever if you can't find them again (spoiler alert: you won't).

Crafted weapons suck compared to legendary items, but legendary weapons are bland. A legendary spear might do bleed damage or cripple. That's about the extent of the coolness. One weapon doesn't lose durability, another is lighter and uses slightly less stamina. They are mostly boring stat sticks. The game doesn't do a good job explaining what makes them special, either. You have to look it up. Huge missed opportunity.

Armor continues to upgrade through crafting, but if you are playing agility, you won't get many bonuses for a long time. If you're an agility and bow enjoyer, you also won't be very helpful. Good luck finding a legendary bow. I found one after 65 hours. It was only 1 damage better than my crafted bow. Actually, that was a lie. I found a bow geared toward strength. That was a kick in the teeth.

When you shoot, random pieces of the landscape, your follower, and even the air itself can stop your shots. Headshots may do more damage, but good luck hitting them. The damage isn't enough to justify the risk of missing such a small target.

But even then, it doesn't matter because you won't really be fighting. Get a named level 4 thrall, and they will fight for you. It becomes a game of Pokémon: you tell them where to go, and they kill things. They take almost no damage from attacks that nearly one-shot you.

But go into the wrong dungeon or area and you will be out-leveled, out-damaged, and out of luck. The game gives no indication whether you are somewhere you should be. I wasn't looking for MMO-style level guides, but entering a dungeon where enemies were using steel arrows and two-shotting me wasn't fun.

In that same dungeon, we found a boss that killed our followers and then us because it was an “end-level” dungeon. No warning. Just fun. Screw you, Cyclopean Halls. So unfun and a complete blindside.

I have so many more issues with this game. It feels incomplete. There is such a cool idea here that could have been amazing, but it isn't fleshed out. Instead of adding basics like a minimap, quest journal, breadcrumbs for the main quest, or better scaling for weapons, armor, and adventures, they just let it all go.

My friend playing with me said, “This was the enhanced version? What was the original like?”

In the end, bad design and poor choices wasted so much potential. No direction across a beautiful, vast map turned what could have been a great adventure into a tedious search for a needle in a haystack. Spending twenty minutes in a dungeon to reach the treasure chest and get two candles and five gold pieces isn't satisfying.

Ultimately, that killed the game for me. Wandering the desert and getting nothing for my trouble wasn't satisfying.

I love this game. Or, rather I love parts of this game. As the reader can tell I've played a lot over the past eight years but while the numbers show dedication, they bely the disappointments that have made me quit now for the third time.

I will tell you what I love and then tell you how I think the game could be made better.

The first fifty hours are pure magic and absorbing. Sitting at the base of a cliff on night one in grass clothing, struggling to build a fire while listening to the distant howling caught my imagination. Some nights, after I had a house I would just sit outside and watch the moon go by. Since the game didn't force me to sleep I would pretend I was sleeping most nights after watching the moon with a drink of some kind.

I loved building fortresses and populating them with thralls. The threat of a purge, although I eventually turned them off, was enough motivation to build them big. In my last game I built five, and some twenty sandstone shacks because I made the sandstorms killers and used a mod that gave a small chance of demons visiting at night unless I had walls. The rationale for the purges is silly. I imagined I was conquering the Exile and Darfari settlements and hung their banners from my walls. If the purges had been the locals revolting my rule....that would have made sense to me.

The progressive difficulty and hope of new tech kept me going. Being able to see what would kill me made me keep my thralls close, search for resources and slowly expand out.

Here is what was is missing that I created in my story: love, needs and backstory. The story needs a love interest and when they die, another comes along, or maybe there are many. My last hero started out being virtuous and became a rake. The game needs to build this in so your players don't have to create it.

Needs: I made them more pronounced. Always sleeping, always keeping on top of hunger and thirst, booze and even better meals and bathing.

Backstory: every thrall I gave a name to and wrote down one or two lines of where they came from and what they did to bring them to the Exiled Lands.

Three reasons I quit. First time was the weak plot. When I learned what the overall goal was I felt like it was shallow vs. the effort. I learned what it was too early in the game and quit after the first visit to the Library. The reveal should be late in the game so the revealer should be in a late game area like the Caldera or on the slopes.
Second, it is too easy to walk into a dungeon that you aren't ready for and without warning you are waking up in your bed with tons of lost equipment and thralls who are now just memories. I felt it was cheating on the designer's parts so had no reservation about figuring out how to restart from an earlier save before my death. The nameless city, shouldn't have world bosses in it for it to serve it's purpose.
Finally, the search for the artefacts is in itself boring. Each artefact should have it's own motivation and a fuller story. A quest to recover each one on its own and in the end to learn you have the ruby slipper would make a better story.

I hope this is helpful for the creators. I'm leaving on a low note whereas if I were leaving on a high note I'd begin another game using a different strategy.

It's been fun. Thank you for making such a wonderful, yet still imperfect, game.

The graphics are nice, the editor for building the base, the house builder, is easy and fun to use.  The character customization has a reasonable variety of options.  The creatures and environment provide interesting challenges for a survival game.  The Conan theme is fun.  However...

To mirror the opening story dialogue in the game, "Where I come from players lose their carefully crafted equipment in battle when they take on a difficult opponent and they are defeated, they do not lose all their equipment when they are offline and due to some unresolved design bugs in the game that occur during updates the players are killed in such a way that all their carefully crafted equipment is unrecoverable."  This is such a known issue that some players have prudently resorted to removing their equipment before logging off and put it in a safe chest.  A player should not have to resort to this sort of game data self defense.

Free survival games, such as Once Human or the paid game Satisfactory do a better job of preserving data than this game.  Although I didn't lose a great deal of equipment encountering this bug in the game design, I could see how players who invested more time and effort in gather their materials and crafting their equipment would be extremely displeased.

Unless the developers make some sort of permanent crate to recover your equipment from such obvious game bugs and/or a Noah's Ark safe starting area when a character has to be relocated due to landscape collision error during an update reset, I can not recommend this game to anyone.  The frustration of losing hours (probably for some players days, and weeks) of your invested time due to bug in the game makes this a game you do not want to spend money on.

I hope this review makes you think twice before investing in this game.

This is coming from a single player, so I have no experience with multiplayer or online servers. I am also not huge on building and prefer adventuring. That being said... I will start with the TL;DR.

Despite all the flaws and me agreeing with most of the negative and critical comments as they are true, I would absolutely recommend this game during a sale. You will get your money's worth even if you just buy the basic game and 0 DLCs. Especially if you are one of those people who love to get lost in the game world. If you are getting lost in statistics, builds and minmaxing, ehh maybe pass this one.

If you are one of those people who sink hundreds of hours into a game and hyperfocus, yes things will start getting a bit frustrating after a while as you start noticing them more but none of it is game breaking or unsolvable with admin commands. 

People say there is no story, but the story is in the background for those who are interested. Similar to The Secret World (rest in peace), there's a lot of conspiracy theory adjacent lore but in this game it's about ancient civilizations and aliens instead of secret societies. It is not obvious lore, a lot of it is implied and you kinda have to piece it together but the parallels are there.

There's a lot of technical improvement in Enhanced over the UE4 version of the game (mainly I noticed fighter thrall AI doing much better), but the visual upgrade is something I wouldn't really call an upgrade. The game looks better to younger folk who are used to the plastic look and floor reflections that make your eyes bleed, but it has lost a lot of its grit, atmosphere and artistic style. 

Performance wise, I apparently have recommended card (3060) but I can't play even on medium settings without stutters and my coolers working overtime. Not a huge deal though because on low it runs great (I only have textures set to high) and it still looks alright. In fact, some of the supposedly enhancing options make it look worse (like the lumen one). 

Some of the stuff you will start noticing after some time and potentially get frustrated with:

Lights are horrendous, and unlike on UE4 they don't light anything. You will be stumbling around in the dark even with a torch, but you can make the night go by really fast in the settings. Water in some places is just a sheet of a dead surface and you won't be able to tell you are underwater aside from your character doing the swimming animation. Starting area big river is not flowing, but has lapping waves like a lake or a sea. Your follower thralls WILL get stuck in the ground occasionally during battles (but that has been improved over time), your battle animals and thralls will sometimes body block you into getting stuck and dying. Some journey steps can get bugged and will require a restart or a mod that resolves them. There's more but it's all on a similar level.

Your character is substantially weaker than your followers once you get good ones, so there is little reason to get involved in combat most of the time aside from spectating and managing potential glitches.   Not a bad thing though, depends on your playstyle but just putting it out there. For example you will have 400-ish HP, and your follower can get up to 4k. Same with damage, thralls are significantly stronger than you if you gear them properly.  

The teleportation system is there, but by the time you get to it you are basically nearing the endgame. Not really useful in my experience unless you want to drag out the gameplay or farm stuff like crazy for whatever purpose (it really isn't needed if you aren't big on building and forever worlds). You either have to build a big map that has obelisks that can transport you to fixed locations (without an option to travel back), or you build sorcery teleporters on key locations that work both ways but give you corruption the farther you travel. I found it easier to just ride my horse around and explore rather than spend time gathering resources and building these teleporters all over the map for locations I would visit once or twice maybe. But there are options for those who want them and find them useful I guess.

The combat isn't that great mechanically and it's fairly easy (once you learn how to time the dodges, blocks and avoid getting stuck in swinging animation while getting pummeled, because mobs do hit hard and you are super squishy no matter what armor you wear). Or just let thralls do the work while you observe from a safe distance lol. However, weapons do have gravity and you will feel your hits connecting in a satisfying way. AND it's fun.

There is a lot to explore, the hand tailored map is done very well and you can climb anything to find treasures or little nooks with lore or emote/recipe unlocks, or minibosses. Dungeons are well made, creatures are cool, progression is interesting (yes you will need a ton of different crafting benches for all your needs, and to hunt down crafting thralls to manage them for bonuses, but that's better part of the game - pokemon with slaves lol)

The atmosphere is still really good and immersive, and you can absolutely sink a ton of hours into this game. Like I said at the tl;dr start, despite all of these things, I recommend grabbing this during a sale. In this day and age of anime and sim slops and games that feel super empty while costing double the price, this one is a keeper. Even if you just run through it once and are done with it.

P.S. I have a LOT more hours in the game, and still decided to buy it at full price.

My SO and I got the base game to give it a try, originally. I think we were 2 hours in when I gave up and said 'no thanks' because it was that bad. I didn't remember why we stopped playing, so recently we tried this game again and I understand why I stopped playing and would not recommend it. 

TL;DR: The game is fun, but is a host to a myriad of bugs/unfair mechanics + blatant, overbearing cash-grab tactics - DO NOT BUY!

- The game allows you to interact with DLC content, but only enough to make you feel as if you need to buy the DLC content. The button in the tech tree "hide DLC content" doesn't actually [i]do[/i] anything. It might hide a few building sets, but does not hide stuff like weapons. Even with DLC content "off", I can still see several sets that require DLC. If I click on those sets to see what their prerequisites are, it says "unowned DLC". If you have a button to turn that stuff off, DLC content should not appear [i]at all[/i] when it's activated. This mostly pertains to armor, weapons, and jewelry sets. Couple this with mobs such as rabbits only being useful if you picked up the Twitch drop for them (which the game DOES NOT tell you about) and it's enough to inspire deep disgust.

The extra "content" is, in my opinion, expensive, considering that all but [i]one[/i] pack appears to be cosmetics only and they are accordingly priced (Isle of Siptah is $19.99 while all other DLC is $9.99). There's also an in-game cash shop with more ridiculously overpriced cosmetic items. Please pick a lane: Overpriced DLC or Overpiced Cash Shop, not both. It says something when their cheapest coin pack is $10 -- the same price as 99% of their DLCs.

- The animal pens and the compost bins work [i]very[/i] slowly even if you turn up crafting station speed, meaning that it's more efficient to loot or abuse the religion system. I'm not even sure that there is a "tamer" type NPC that you can grab to speed things up because I haven't seen one yet.

I would like to see this NPC system reworked so that everyone has skills with some being higher than others a la Soulmask. With this system, they would still have "Master" skills such as cooking/fighting, but you could also slot an NPC into any other task until you find a more suitable replacement. Slotting an NPC to a crafting table they aren't suited for would give you a 2x boost to speed, but you wouldn't get access to things like items with stat bonuses or special recipes -- only a suitable NPC could do that.

- Raising certain stats feels like it does nothing. For example, if you raise the stat that affects your stamina, you get a bigger stamina pool, but stamina runs out very quickly no matter what you do. Add to this that climbing itself is buggy and it feels like your only option is to turn on Creative Mode and fly to where you need to go. This is where traversal tools would be insanely helpful without trivializing content. After all, Enshrouded managed to do this just fine and I think that Conan Exiles could, too. You could argue that sorcery does this, but in my experience sorcery has been useful exactly zero times. The payoff for the amount of drawbacks you suffer make it even [i]less[/i] useful.

What I do like about stats is that when you reach a certain level, you're allowed to make a choice that affects that stat. For example, reaching level 10 in (I think) Expertise will allow you to choose between getting double drops from harvesting or getting more rare resources.

- As I said, climbing itself is finicky and kind of broken. Half of the time you'll grab a cliff face or other climbable object immediately. The other half of the time you're going to waste a substantial amount of stamina trying to get your character to latch on. (Note: the game will tell you if what you're trying to climb isn't valid, so this complaint is tied to things that you [i]can[/i] climb.) You'll also find that if you reach the top of a wall or cliff, your character won't detach and will instead keep climbing. 

What I do like about the climbing system is that you're allowed to jump off a cliff, turn mid-air, grab the cliff face and slide to slow your descent. This is one of the few things that this game has done well.

- Building is both a joy and a pain. All of the building sets actually look [i]really[/i] nice, but like other games have done, they put one texture on the front and another texture on the back of certain wall sets. This means that you can't build anything that looks cohesive on the inside, unless you want to stick to building [i]only[/i] with sandstone or simple boxes with no interior dividing walls. Snapping is finicky to the point of pain, especially with foundations and roofs. Chests also have range meaning that it's always better to over-encumber yourself to build, rather than storing everything in a chest and building from there. I would love to see an expanded chest range and "interior" items that match the texture that's on the back of walls or the ability to apply an item to a wall that changes its texture.

- Enemies can and will stunlock you into oblivion, but you can't stunlock them. I think it's only fair that if an enemy can use a special attack multiple times without apparently using any stamina, you should be able to do the same to them. They also seem to have ultra precision and never miss a shot, even if they're low tier and low level. This fact is being used as a means of making the game artificially harder than it actually is. I don't mind difficult enemies; I mind BS tactics.

- In instanced dungeons there are lootable chests placed in spots that you can get [i]to[/i] but can't get back [i]from.[/i] This requires you to die and return to the start of the dungeon. This is where traversal tools would be most useful. If Enshrouded can make a grappling hook useful without trivializing their dungeons, so can Conan Exiles. (You could argue sorcery, but sorcery was specifically not allowed in the dungeon we were in and therefore cannot be counted as a traversal tool. This was actually the first thing we tried.)

- Inventory management is absolute [i]balls.[/i] Certain wooden boxes come with presets for certain item types. The larger chests don't have this and there doesn't seem to be an easy way to make them only accept stuff like plant items. The type of stuff they accept also seems kind of random. Why are bugs not considered a type of plant item, considering we get bugs from harvesting bushes? Why do we not have a chest category specifically for items that are consumable or foodstuffs?

Personal inventory is also tiny, which makes loot gremlins like me incredibly sad. Why are you giving me access to so many chests if you don't want me to loot them?

Thusly, inventory management desperately needs a total rework so that [i]all[/i] chests can be set to only accept items of a certain type. I also think that if you put points into the stat that raises your carrying capacity, you should be getting more personal inventory slots every so often. +2 or 3 slots for every 5-10 levels of stat increase seems pretty fair to me.

- Journeys are enjoyable, however they do not recognize when you've already done a thing. For example, if you've already completed an objective (e.g. placing a wall and floor), the game will not recognize that and you'll have to do everything twice. Sometimes this is an easy fix, but other times it's more of a pain than it's worth. Ideally, if you 'start' a journey and have already done the quest objectives, the game should sense that and reward you accordingly.

The thing is, the modding community has already taken care of a lot of these problems. However, a game [i]should not[/i] be relying on its community to fix issues that they have been vocal about. A good game should take the criticism and strive to improve which Conan Exiles is decidedly [i]not[/i] doing. That, combined with their blatant cash-grab tactics and unfair mechanics is why I would not recommend this game.

The reason I give it a negative review is because the game’s development over nearly a decade has done little to address its Pain Points – elements of the game that make it more confusing and difficult, not due to game design but due to the inability of its developers to perceive errors and oversights in its user interface and implementation. Subsequent development of the game’s features lack coherence and further make the game’s UI evermore obtuse.

Further, development has also focused on toxic dopamine addiction delivery and less on individual player expression. The telling signs of this are two features:

RNG
Also known as Random Interval Reward Schedules, RNG is a way of extending content at no development cost. It’s something between a shoulder shrug and a raised middle finger. Its effects on players are less benign. In making a player repeat the same actions ad nauseam hoping for a different result, it mirrors the definition of insanity while forcing players to chase the dopamine hit. Players are not playing because they want to; they’re playing because they feel they must and have been conditioned by the game industry to regard this as normal. It’s been given a very normal sounding name: farming.

Legendary Uber Items
Itemization has always posed a threat to cooperation in multiplayer games but only if it allows a player to become nearly invincible. Most players of Conan Exiles play the game solo. Thus the ability to create evermore powerful weapons and armor is essential. However, when developer created super items – items more powerful than any player can hope to craft – are introduced, it diminishes the control players have over their progression. And, finally, these uber items are kept behind an RNG wall, adding them to the toxic cycle of the game playing you rather than you playing the game. 

Nonetheless, Conan Exiles is so compelling that a large community of mod developers assumed the task of addressing its stark shortcomings and senseless difficulties. Thus developed a strange and abusive codependence. Mods make the game more appealing and playable. The developers both realize and resent this, creating updates that break mods, often so needlessly that it can only be interpreted as intentional. 

Despite all the negatives, as the whole sticks and stones and plants gathering genre goes, Conan Exiles can be great fun, though addictive to an unhealthy degree. It’s that addictive quality – the game’s ability to deliver doses of dopamine with regularity and in short-and long-term forms – that feeds the abusive relationship between developers, who rarely play the game, and players who can’t stop playing. It’s the dealer/junkie relationship.

Conan Exiles is a geezer game, meaning its mechanics allow older players to experience success. To achieve this the game relies on the player acquiring followers to aid in crafting and combat. Inspired less by Robert E. Howard’s Conan stories, and more by a Dino De Laurentiis B Movie from 1982, it’s oddly violent, bloody, and brutal. You gain followers by clubbing them senseless and torturing them on a Wheel of Pain – a feature of the film – until they become your thrall. Oddly, through a series of updates added over the years, other ways were added to acquire thralls. You can hire them with gold from a bar, free them from prisoner cages, or even earn their loyalty through quests though this last option is quite limited and only applies to two fighters. This makes the whole torture mechanic feel even more bizarre.

Most brutal is the peculiar sorcery system. Although it offers few features, regarded as optional, most players feel compelled to acquire sorcery which requires graphic human sacrifice. 

There is no ability to allow you to heal an ally. Like UO there are bandages but no ability to apply a bandage to another. In short, no cross healing. And like the early multiplayer fantasy games of over 40 years ago, no ability to give anything to anybody without a poorly implemented trade window. Most players opt for putting items into chests and then allow the other player access to the chest.

Fast travel options are absurd and largely addressed through mods. Mounts are awkward, particularly to anyone using a controller instead of a keyboard.

In short, there’s a wonderful game here trapped in a distortion field created by its developers in Oslo, Norway. Were they to deemphasize RNG, commission a third-party Pain Point analysis, implement its findings, and employ focus group testers to deliver feedback on the UI, this game could achieve its potential. 

As it is, however, with its reliance on modders who are alternately embraced and thwarted, Conan Exiles fails to feel like a commercial video game in full release. Fewer than half its players stick with it. Less than a third complete its beginner dungeon. Although far from dying, it has the feel of someone adjusting the picture frames in a house that’s on fire.

My review about Conan Exiles applies not just for Conan Exiles Enhanced edition, but to Legacy as well. Although mainly the review is going for Conan Exlles, its generally a major complaint for Funcom throughout their decades long experience in game development. And yes, looking at my gameplay time, its a love-hate relationship.

"Funcom Jank" is a term that been thrown around for people who played their games throughout their existance. Conan Exiles does not escape from this term, not even their newest Dune : Awakening got spared from it. 

Conan Exiles primarily focuses on the combat mechanic in almost everything you do in game. By far it's also the most broken, most unrefined combat system that ever existed in game history. I have played Gothic the original, one of the most unfavorable combat mechanic ever. It's slow, it's stiff. The remake have that essence of the orignal, but it's a lot more smoothed out. Conan Exiles basically inherited the Gothic original combat jank. Slow, stiff, and for some reason have that "heroic pause" after an attack and locked in that animation (very noticeable from warhammer) if you do not dodge out of it, making you vulnerable to attacks by other mobs or boss in the vicinity and use more than appropriate stamina needed.
In close combat, literally kissing the enemies, your attack with long reach weapons like greatsword, spears, polearm, warhammer, greataxe, can still miss. An enemy with a club or dagger which in common sense, have no reach can hit you as far as a spear or pike can. Since enemies does not relies or needed the stamina gauge like a player do, they can just keep spamming heavy attack while tracking you perfectly even after you dodge them, stun-locking you constantly without missing.
Switching locked-on target requires you to move your mouse instead of a button press. No game ever done this, and for me caused disorientation and headache. This is the main reason I refuse to use the locked-on system, because it's more of a hindrance than helping, even though that is what the system was suppose to do, helping a player, became the most redundant system implemented.

Giant enemies movements and orientation was funny at the first 1-3 times it happened, but it continues to happen all the time.  The giant alligators world boss? You are suddenly inside it's snout. If you are lucky, you'll be on top of it. Luckiest if it flew into the air and dissapeared, refreshed it's hp and suddenly you lose 70% of your health from their attack that came out of nowhere. You take 3-4 rolls to get behind the King Rhino's side/back, it took no time to suddenly facing you and ram you accross the map. Good luck to even try landing an attack on the Rocknose King, because that guy interupts your movement every single attack it does. You'd be kising the floor 90% of the whole combat and your only way to damage it is to use a ranged weapon.

This is the jank that I am talking about, coming from a company that have more than 3 decade experience making videogames. Don't give me the "Oh it's Funcom, their game have never been perfect, the jank is to be expected". That does not give them the pass to release a product that seems like it's made by an amature developer. It's like saying the bugs in Bathesda game is normal and to be expected, its okay to be released as a full price product. Funcom refuse to improve themselves, fixing what's broken but asking for a ton of money for not even mediocre game, it's not even triple A material. The modding community is actually saving and making the game enjoyable to players, but every update for some reason is just another way of them saying "keep the game broken and unenjoyable, screw you".

If you want a game to lose some time into, Conan Exiles in singleplayer is actually okay to play with, the environment is beautiful, the setting is breathtaking even though it can feel empty for such a big map, the building mechanic is okay and need some smoothing but still relaxing. Having said that, prepare to experience a very harrowing gameplay you will ever had in your gaming history.

Conan Exiles is a survival crafting game that can be played either solo or multiplayer on a server. Set in the Conan universe there is an emphasize on being "savage" and living in a harsh world. You'll be gathering resources, base building, crafting, fighting and exploring.

Ultimately I wanted to like this game but ended up bouncing off. I actually really like the aesthetic and world they have presented here, one where creatures are dangerous and vile, and people are even worse. Not only do the horrible enemies you take down engage in slavery and cannibalism, but you can too! Its a cruel world and you need to be cruel to survive. 

The problem is gameplay though. Combat is not great. feeling clunky to me. Crafting progression also felt off to me, where you seem to make big progress all around the "noob" river in the beginning, but then need to travel through fairly empty and not very interesting land to look for ways to advance. Things like magic are pretty hidden and not very obvious which isn't a bad thing by itself, but unfortunately exploring is not very interesting. The world feels like an old MMO, with large open spaces with enemies just kind of standing around and no real level design to speak off. So there is this tension, where there are resources you want to find, like characters that give you abilities, new metals, and even stories, but actually going through the world is a chore. There are things worth finding but the act of finding them sucks. 

The balance also feels off. While you can can edit XP rates, combat difficulty, resource requirements and so on, I strongly feel that it shouldn't be up to me to figure out how to make the game fun. Even the official servers do not use the default settings. My complaint isn't that you can edit these things, but rather that the suggested defaults are not really fun and you will want to tinker with them if you actually intend to play.

Overall I do think I will try to return to this game in the future, and maybe with a solid group I could eventually get hooked, but as of right now the actual gameplay just left me cold even though I appreciated what the world was trying to do.

There is a lot to love here. The building system alone is fantastic. You can make a little survival shack, a sprawling fortress, a gothic castle, or basically whatever architectural fever dream you have in mind. Building our base was one of my favorite parts of the game, and I genuinely never felt like I was running out of things I wanted to add or change.

The thrall system is another huge highlight. There is something incredibly satisfying about capturing an NPC, dragging them back to your base, putting them on the Wheel of Pain, and eventually turning them into a heavily armed employee who will defend your stuff. And once you have the companion system going, the game gets even more fun. Running around with two thralls and casually murdering our way through entire villages was ridiculous in the best possible way. The animals are fun too, although I definitely preferred the human companions. Being able to equip your thralls with actual armor and weapons makes them feel much more useful and customizable. The animals are still great to have around the base, though, and they add some personality to your little house.

The tavern system was probably one of my favorite additions. Watching the base slowly become a place that actually felt lived in was fantastic. Instead of just having a collection of crafting stations and storage boxes, suddenly there were people wandering around, drinking, talking, and generally making the place feel like an actual settlement. It sounds like a small thing, but it made a huge difference.

Exploration is also a lot of fun. The world has a great variety of environments, from deserts and forests to frozen areas and volcanic regions, and there is always something dangerous lurking around the corner. The combat is satisfying, too. You have melee weapons, archery, mounts, sorcery (although its intuitiveness left a lot to be desired), and your companions, there are plenty of ways to approach a fight.

The boss fights, however, were extremely hit or miss for us. Some bosses felt surprisingly easy, while others seemed to have decided that we personally offended them and needed to be erased from existence. Even with some of the best gear available, the purple power guy in the cave maze place absolutely destroyed us. We went in feeling pretty confident and came out looking like we had just been personally humbled by the concept of that bosses personal space.

The base raids were another feature I really enjoyed. There is something satisfying about preparing a defensive base and then watching everything you've built get tested. It also gives your massive, ridiculous fortress a purpose beyond simply looking cool. We didn't get to build ours perfect, but i bet when you do its so SWEET!

I also really appreciated how many server and gameplay settings you can customize. We changed some of the settings to reduce how quickly weapons and food deteriorated, and honestly, it made the experience much more enjoyable for us. I like having the option to tailor the survival mechanics rather than being forced into one specific level of grind.

And yes, there is a grind. A pretty substantial one. Gathering resources, maintaining equipment, upgrading your base, and generally keeping everything running can become a job in itself. The game also does very little to actually explain what you're supposed to be doing. There isn't a nice, convenient quest log holding your hand and telling you where to go next. Eventually you reach the point where you either start experimenting constantly or go searching online for answers, and I really don't enjoy having to hunt down guides just to figure out what the game expects me to do.

That's probably where my biggest problem with Conan Exiles comes in.

I had a very similar feeling playing this as I did with Smalland. There are so many genuinely great ideas here, and so many systems that I really enjoyed, but by the end I couldn't shake the feeling that the game was unfinished. Not necessarily lacking content, because there is a ridiculous amount of content, but unfinished in how those pieces come together. There are bugs, janky AI moments, questionable pathfinding, occasional multiplayer weirdness, and plenty of little things that make the whole experience feel rough around the edges.

The lack of direction is a big part of that for me. I don't mind a game letting me figure things out for myself, but Conan Exiles sometimes crosses the line from discover the world into go Google what the hell you're supposed to be doing. And once I'm doing that FOR EVERYTHING, I'm kinda done.

Still, I had a really good time with Conan Exiles. Building was fantastic, the thralls were hilarious and useful, the world was fun to explore, the combat was satisfying, and turning our base into a ridiculous little civilization was incredibly rewarding. The tavern especially made the whole place feel alive in a way I wasn't expecting.

I just wish the game felt a little more polished and complete. There is an excellent survival game buried in Conan Exiles, and for the most part, I had a blast digging it out. I just wish I didn't have to dig quite so deep.

Cool mishmash of ideas and gameplay influences that somehow works surprisingly well. The game looks and plays wonderfully, and the world around you is incredibly varied and pleasing to look at. Deserts, tropical areas, snowy peaks, ancient ruins. There are many places and locations to explore, and exploring them is genuinely fun. In one cave you might find a boss, in another a spellbook, and in a third a whole bunch of spiders.
The thrall system is just incredible. Capturing people and then putting them to work gives you a real sense of interacting with your own group or village of inhabitants, much more so than in most other survival games with similar mechanics. Even though the system can sometimes feel a little clunky. You have to place each follower manually, and when moving them you have to carry them one at a time, or two at a time if you have upgraded the relevant skill.
The building system is simply fantastic. It is very simple, while still being varied enough to let you build pretty much any castle or fortress you want, as long as you are willing to grind for the necessary resources.
The magic system is also great. Even at the earliest levels, it provides noticeable and satisfying bonuses, mostly useful for exploration and navigating the world. Creating ice bridges, locating ore, removing fall damage, and so on.
The game does, however, have this slightly unpleasant feeling of an online MMO, early janky survival games, and, strangely enough, Rust. From MMOs it takes grindy progression system, with professions and skills locked behind level caps. It gets almost ridiculous at times. Some regions in the game has its own temperature system, (borrowed from Zelda), and to deal with it you need good armor. Good armor that you have to craft yourself, and you cannot craft necessary equipment until you are approaching level 50, by which point you are already close to the level cap. Leveling up your followers is especially tedious, since they can only gain experience through combat.
From janky survival games, Conan inherits an overwhelming amount of text in its menus. The menus themselves are extremely confusing and unintuitive, along with a barrage of mechanics that are either poorly explained or not explained at all. Although, in a way, figuring out how to craft a particular item has always been part of the genre.
From Rust, the game seems to have borrowed its building system, bedrolls, and endless resource farming. Building is not cheap, especially when you start constructing things out of reinforced materials and so on. If you have played Rust, you will quickly notice many smaller similarities and borrowed ideas.
And of course, you cannot ignore the absolutely awful monetization. A huge portion of the game's content is locked behind DLC, which, as always, is a terrible practice.
In the end, it is clear that Conan Exiles has taken a lot from other games, both positive and negative. And while I have plenty of criticism to throw at it, and its flaws often outweigh its strengths, I cannot honestly call it a bad game. Even with its grindy mechanics and awful, predatory monetization, it is still an incredibly addictive and interesting experience that is genuinely fun to dive into, either alone or with friends. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys survival games.

This is a difficult one. There's much to love and to enjoy  but there's also much jank which throws off the immersion and gameplay over all and that's a shame really. But as there's no option other than to recommend this game or not, this makes rating the game hard.

But it's very much like LOTR online. Such a great Franchise and fantasy world deserve much better. They deserve AAA quality games and animation, due their scope and following and this is not it.  Although all of the components are in the game,  gore, building, survival, combat, none of them are done particularly well in my opinion. Don't get me wrong they're done ok and there is fun to be had but it just doesn't quite hit the spot or scratch that Conan itch properly.

As an example - take the combat, There is gore, I mean you can cut people in half, over and over again but it's just missing ....something. You see the same kill animation most times over and over. Combat seem to be to me get the first hit in and then you'll be able to just keep hitting for most enemies. It doesn't feel very tactical or very real and although some of the animations are ok, again they're not always great or there aren't that many of them. if there are going to by kill animations there need to be loads for EVERY WEAPON - not just one to two each. The combat just doesn't feel great IMO which is one of the biggest problems in a game world known for such. It's like most things in the game - it just needs to be better, with more weight, better parrying and dodging etc, more kicks, punches, head butts, better closer camera, less cutting people in half and more realism.

Another example is the character models. We want hugely detailed character models which look amazing and give us the character the Conan universe deserves but there a bit meh, not very detailed, a little duff looking etc.

Take the climbing, the actual climbing animation is nice (although not very varied) but it's integration is shoddy. And horses too - nice to have but look and play a little bit duff.

And that's the same kind of summary to most other parts of the game - they're ok but just not great which sums up this game nicely I think. Some great content and some good gameplay but the implementation is as I've said a little shoddy

It's a shame because Funcom should be applauded for some of the things they've done recently and all for FREE - ie the graphical update (but again it's good but not right up there with or even close to the best)

So that would be my review and my advice to Funcom - you have one of the most amazing and loved franchises, you really could have the most amazing game on your hands with the right focus and with the right changes all completed to an outstanding standard, players would flock in I'm sure. But it just seems to me that instead of everything being done to a 100% amazing standard / competency -  no more than 60-70% competency is achieved.

Come on Funcom this could be amazing with much improved animations (mo cap), blending and an outstanding combat model. Better  and much more detailed character, hair and armour models are definitely needed.

There are recent examples of where all of these things have been done exceedingly well in the last few years. Come on funcom you need more ambition with such a fantastic franchise.
